Subject: Zenline pilot — deployment traffic deconstruction

Alex —

Thanks for hopping on the call earlier. To move the Dedicated proposal forward we need a compact traffic snapshot and a couple of clarifying questions so our sizing is aligned with your real-world mix. I attached a small CSV sample (recent 24h, anonymized IDs) — can you confirm the values below or correct them?

Short checklist:
- Peak concurrent sessions (observed, not theoretical) in a 1-minute window: ?
- Typical conversational depth (turns/session): ?
- Prompt lengths (tokens) distribution: median / p95 / max
- Average assistant response length (tokens) and p95
- Percentage of requests that call external tools or invoke function-calls (approx)
- SLA target for 99th latency for first token and full-response (ms)

If easier, reply inline to the CSV rows. Goal: we want to map concurrency -> session affinity -> GPU packing to give you a realistic committed capacity + burst cushion.

Next steps on our side: Marissa will sketch a partitioning plan (tenant vs pooled), and Ben will propose a burst-CPU/GPU mix for the pilot. If we can lock the traffic numbers by end of week we can include a conservative SKU list in the draft contract.

Attachments: zenline_sample_traffic.csv (24h anonymized), zenline_sla_expectations.pdf (baseline)

Thanks,
Chloe

Chloe —

Thanks for the note and the CSV. Quick answers inline:
- Peak concurrent sessions (1-min observed): 1,200 (we see this during North American morning surge)
- Conversational depth: median 3 turns, p95 12 turns, max observed 48
- Prompt lengths (tokens): median 45, p95 320, max 1,100
- Assistant response length (tokens): average 120, p95 1,000
- Function-calls/tooling: ~18% (most are light metadata fetches; ~2% trigger heavier external lookups)
- SLA target: 99th-first-token 120ms, full-response p99 within 1.8s (for typical <500 token responses)

Attached a slightly expanded CSV sample with headers (we redacted user ids). We also included a column for request_type (chat vs generation) which you might find helpful.

Couple of notes: we batch some user requests client-side (5–10s windows) for cost reasons — that can affect observed concurrency vs incoming requests. Happy to elaborate if that matters for the model of concurrency you use.

—Alex
Alex Rivera
Head of Platform | Zenline AI
alex@zenline.ai

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Zenline pilot — deployment traffic deconstruction

Alex / Chloe —

Thanks Alex — the numbers are very helpful. A few follow-ups that directly map to how we'll size the Dedicated pools and packing heuristics:

1) Session lifespan and KV cache: Do sessions keep a persistent KV cache per session for the duration of the conversation? If yes, how long do sessions typically remain active when idle? (minutes/hours)

2) Cold-start tolerance: For the 1200 concurrent peak, how many are warm with cached KV vs cold? Approx percentage?

3) Tokenization and model family: Which model family are you planning to serve for this pilot (open-llama / mixin / custom finetune)? If you have a preferred quantization profile (8-bit, 4-bit), note it — it changes packing density materially.

4) Burst shaping: You mentioned client-side batching — can you share the typical batch window (ms/s) and whether your client sometimes flushes partial batches on timeout?

5) Mixed-priority routing: Do you have a subset of traffic that requires reserved low-latency routing (e.g., top-tier customers) vs background generation? If so, approximate 
percentage that needs hard SLAs.

If it's helpful I included an example mapping below that we'll use once we get answers:
- Observed concurrency -> target active sessions per GPU (packing)
- KV cache warm ratio -> extra RAM cushion per GPU
- p95 prompt/response tokens -> throughput tokens/s per GPU estimate

Can you reply with the KV cache behavior and cold/warm split? If you prefer a quick call we can run through a short walk-through tomorrow.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Senior Product Manager, Dedicated | Redwood Inference
marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com

From: Alex Rivera <alex@zenline.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>, Chloe Martin <chloe.martin@redwoodinference.com>
Cc: procurement@zenline.ai
Date: 2026-08-23T08:42:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Zenline pilot — deployment traffic deconstruction

Marissa —

Good questions — answers below:

1) KV cache: Yes, we maintain a per-session KV cache. Idle timeout is ~15 minutes by default; mobile sessions are shorter (~8 minutes) due to network churn.

2) Warm vs cold at peak: Rough estimate 68% warm, 32% cold (clients with long conversations keep warm caches).

3) Model family: We'll start with a trimmed-open Llama variant (quantized 4-bit) for most customers. For a small subset (~10%) we plan to run a larger finetuned 8-bit model for high-quality responses.

4) Client batching: Typical batch window 800ms; client flushes on 1.5s timeout. We occasionally bump flush to 300ms during high-latency mobile conditions.

5) Priority split: ~14% of traffic is marked high-priority and needs low-latency reserved paths.

Attaching an export with session-level warm/cold flags and a short readme describing our batching heuristics.

—Alex
Alex Rivera
Head of Platform | Zenline AI

Attachments: zenline_session_flags_export.csv, batching_readme.txt

Alex —

This is excellent, thank you. Summary and proposed action items: 

Summary (what we heard)
- Peak concurrency: 1,200 (68% warm)
- Conversational depth: median 3 / p95 12
- Token shapes: median prompt 45 / p95 320 / max 1,100; avg response 120 / p95 1,000
- Client batching: 800ms typical; flushes at 1.5s timeout
- Priority traffic: ~14% requires reserved low-latency routing
- Models: primary 4-bit Llama variant; 10% on larger 8-bit finetuned model

Action items
1) Marissa: produce a two-scenario capacity sketch by EOD Monday — Conservative (commit + 20% burst) and Aggressive (commit + 50% burst). Include GPU SKU mapping and RAM cushions for KV caches.
2) Ben: run a token-throughput microbenchmark for the two model profiles and include expected tokens/s and expected p99 tail impact.
3) Chloe/CS: we'll prepare an initial SLA appendix that separates reserved low-latency lanes (14%) from best-effort pool.

Next milestone: internal sizing doc and SKU list for the commercial draft (target Wed). We'll also add the CSV exports you provided to the HubSpot deal record.

If that plan looks right, I'll mark this thread for the deal folder and schedule a 30-minute sync with product + tech tomorrow at 10am PT.

Thanks again — looking forward to locking numbers.

Chloe
